Both factual checkable claims in the tweet are wrong; a corrective note is appropriate. Provisional 'no note needed' likely reflected the rhetorical-question framing (raters thought 'it's just a question'), but the rhetorical form still asserts both factual premises and the tweet is widely shared (479K impressions).

Citing CNN/NBC/ABC on the suspect and Wikipedia / a county-level vote source on Utah County partisanship is the bar. FAIL if the note: (a) only addresses one of the two false premises; (b) calls Robinson a Republican or claims his ideology firmly (the evidence is messier — anti-fascist messages on ammo, but inactive/unaffiliated voter); (c) repeats the framing 'Dem area' as if accurate. Must avoid the original note's structure that the reference note essentially nails — so the original is actually a good model here.

A correct note acknowledges uncertainty on both sides: the specific coma/amputation claim is unconfirmed, while officials say he is injured but alive. FAIL if it endorses the coma/amputation as confirmed, or if it has no source.

The Saudi FM only says patience is not unlimited and they reserve the right to respond IF attacked — a defensive caveat, not an offer to join an offensive US-Israel war on Iran. The tweet's 'officially threatened to join' framing misrepresents the source, so a corrective note is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note corrects the specific overstatement: there is no official Arab/GCC statement threatening to JOIN the US-Israel offensive against Iran; Gulf leaders affirmed they are not participating and are prioritizing defense, diplomacy, and de-escalation (a reserved right to self-defense if attacked is not the same as joining the war). It should ideally note the attached clip itself says Gulf states 'would defend their territories but not attack Iran.' The note must NOT deny that the conflict / Gulf ministerial meeting is real. A note that endorses the 'Arabs joining the war' framing, or that just calls it fake without the joining-vs-defending distinction, should FAIL. Cite credible reporting (Al Jazeera, Fox, etc.).

tweet_summary: A small account (6.4k followers) quote-tweets a praising post about an essay and complains 'someone publishing an AI-written article' is bad — but the underlying essay is excerpted from a real Times of India blog post 'The quiet grief of adult friendship' by Pranav Jain.
why_note_decision: The tweet's central claim — that the essay is AI-written — is a subjective stylistic judgment, not a verifiable fact. Multiple comments in the thread point to AI 'tells' (sentence fragments, full-stop cadence) but these are heuristics, not proof. The essay exists under Pranav Jain's byline at TOI's 'Civil Irony' blog; the author hasn't disclosed AI use, but absence of disclosure also doesn't prove it's human-written. Either way, this is opinion/framing — a stylistic critique, not a checkable factual claim a reader is being deceived about. The original note's framing ('no indication it is AI-generated') is also not a verifiable counter-claim — current detectors are unreliable.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The essay's authorship attribution to Pranav Jain at TOI is real and verifiable; whether AI was involved in drafting is unknowable from outside and is a stylistic judgment, not a checkable fact. Any note that confidently asserts the essay is (or is not) AI-written FAILS — there is no reliable way to prove this from current evidence, and the AI-vs-human debate is the subjective complaint the tweet is making. A note simply pointing to the TOI byline would also FAIL because that doesn't address the substantive 'is this AI?' question and isn't the kind of correction worth elevating.
original_note_text: The shared essay is an excerpt from a blog post titled "The quiet grief of adult friendship" by Pranav Jain, with no indication it is AI-generated. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/civil-irony/the-quiet-grief-of-adult-friendship
failure_reason: Note tries to refute an inherently unverifiable claim (whether the essay was AI-drafted) by saying 'no indication' — but absence of indication isn't evidence of absence. The 'AI-written' claim is stylistic/opinion, not a factual claim a note can adjudicate. Raters flagged 'missing key points' (4) and 'incorrect' (3) — likely because the note doesn't really address the tweet's complaint.
importance_lens_rationale: Small-account stylistic debate about AI-vs-human writing. Low world-impact.

tweet_summary: Using a Copernicus 1995-2024 temperature-trend map, the author claims annual mean temperature in 'every country' has been rising 1-1.5 degrees per decade, but India is an 'anomaly' warming less than the rest of the world.
why_note_decision: The headline statistic is false: global mean warming is ~0.27 C/decade (1996-2025, ERA5), and the map's own scale tops out at 2 C/decade with most land at ~0.2-0.6 — nowhere near '1-1.5 C/decade for every country.' That quantified error is checkable and worth correcting. However, the tweet's secondary thrust (India warming less than the global average — an 'anomaly') is broadly TRUE per the data, so a correct note must fix the rate without falsely 'rebutting' the India point. A note IS warranted, but the original note got the India direction backwards and is itself incorrect.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note corrects the false rate — global warming is roughly 0.2-0.3 C/decade, NOT 1-1.5 C/decade, and the map's color scale shows this. The note must NOT repeat the original note's error of claiming India warmed FASTER than the global average (~0.5 C/decade) — that is wrong; India is among the slower-warming land regions (~0.15-0.2 C/decade per IPCC), so the tweet's 'India is an anomaly / warmed less' framing is actually broadly correct. A correct note fixes the per-decade number while NOT contradicting that India warmed below the global average. FAIL any note that asserts India warmed faster/'rather than the least,' or that denies the global rate is far below 1 C/decade.
reference_note: The per-decade figure is overstated: global mean surface warming is about 0.2-0.3 C/decade (Copernicus/ERA5 puts 1996-2025 at ~0.27 C/decade), not 1-1.5 C/decade — the map's scale confirms most land sits around 0.2-0.6 C/decade. India is indeed among the lower-warming land regions (~0.15-0.2 C/decade per IPCC), so it does warm below the global average. https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-indicators/temperature
original_note_text: The map shows global average warming of 0.26°C per decade from 1995-2024, not 1-1.5°C/decade; India warmed faster than this average (~0.5°C/decade) rather than the least. https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-indicators/temperature
failure_reason: Half right, half wrong: correctly debunks the '1-1.5 C/decade' rate, but its second clause ('India warmed faster... rather than the least, ~0.5 C/decade') is incorrect — India warms slower than the global average (~0.15-0.2 C/decade per IPCC), so the tweet's 'India is an anomaly' point is actually broadly true. Reporters tagged it Incorrect (dominant) for this reversed India claim.
importance_lens_rationale: 355k impressions; climate-data literacy matters for progress, and both the tweet's inflated rate and the note's reversed India claim distort the science — a precise correction has real educational value.

tweet_summary: Geopolitics account 'MonitorX' shares purported leaked Israeli MoD/IDF documents claiming the 'Samson Option' includes specific nuclear-strike targets in US cities (LA, NY, Colorado/NORAD), Moscow, Beijing, Berlin, etc., with delivery methods and kiloton yields.
why_note_decision: The 'leaked' documents are widely regarded as a fabrication: native Hebrew speakers in the comments call out broken Hebrew grammar and obvious forgery markers; no credible news outlet or fact-checker authenticated the leak; the only sources circulating it are conspiracy/fringe outlets (State of the Nation, The People's Voice, vtforeignpolicy). The genuine 'Samson Option' is a deterrence doctrine (per Seymour Hersh's book and academic literature) — not a published target list with cities and yields. Treating these graphics as a real IDF document misleads ~450k impressions worth of readers into believing Israel has a written plan to nuke US cities. A correction is clearly warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) flags that the screenshotted 'IDF Samson Option targets' document is unverified / appears fabricated (Hebrew errors, no chain of custody, only fringe outlets are circulating it), AND (b) distinguishes the genuine 'Samson Option' doctrine (a last-resort deterrence concept discussed in Seymour Hersh's 1991 book) from a literal published target list with kiloton yields. Strong notes will cite Wikipedia's Samson Option article for the doctrine and note the absence of any mainstream verification of the 'leak.' Notes that simply repeat 'this is unverified' without addressing the fabrication signals are weaker but acceptable. Notes that TREAT the document as real should FAIL. Notes that argue the doctrine doesn't exist at all should also FAIL (it does, as deterrence theory).
reference_note: The images of an 'IDF Samson Option target list' are not from any verified leak — no mainstream outlet or fact-checker has authenticated them, and Hebrew speakers note grammatical errors consistent with a forgery. The real 'Samson Option' is a deterrence doctrine described in Seymour Hersh's 1991 book, not a published list of US/Russian/Chinese city targets with yields. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samson_Option
original_note_text: Misleading: the 'Samson Option' is described as a last-resort deterrent against existential regional threats, not documented plans to strike US or allied cities. The posted 'leak' is unverified and has been flagged as likely fabricated by analysts. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samson_Option https://x.com/grok/status/1934690310380245085
failure_reason: Sources are weak (Wikipedia + a Grok x.com post — raters tagged 'sources missing/unreliable' 10x). The forgery signals (Hebrew errors, no chain of custody) aren't named explicitly. Note's reasoning is OK but its citation quality is too weak to convince skeptical raters.
importance_lens_rationale: 447k impressions of a fabricated 'leaked IDF nuclear targeting' document stoking war/conspiracy narratives at a sensitive geopolitical moment. Correcting fabricated war documents is exactly the highest-value use of community notes.

why_note_decision: A note is warranted: 'voted to defund ICE' mischaracterizes a no-vote on a broad package. Massie was the only Republican to vote against the January 2026 DHS funding bill, which bundled ~$10B for ICE with funding for many other agencies. Framing a 'no' on the whole package as 'defund ICE' is misleading, and a reader benefits from the actual vote context.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note clarifies that Massie's vote was against a broad January 2026 DHS funding package (which happened to include ICE funding among much else), and that his stated objection was to other provisions (e.g. CISA / censorship concerns), NOT a vote to defund ICE or oppose immigration enforcement. It should cite the roll call / DHS bill and stay neutral. FAIL if the note endorses the 'voted to defund ICE' framing, asserts Massie is anti-ICE, argues the broader merits of Massie's politics, or omits that the bill was an omnibus DHS package rather than an ICE-specific defunding measure. tweet_summary: Claims Dairy Queen 'no longer' meets the FDA criteria for real ice cream and frames polysorbate 80 as a sinister 'chemotherapy chemical'. Embedded TikTok-style video reinforces the framing.
why_note_decision: Two checkable misleading claims. (1) DQ soft serve never qualified as 'ice cream' under FDA's 10% milkfat rule — it has always been ~5% milkfat, marketed as soft serve. 'No longer' implies a recent change that didn't happen. (2) Polysorbate 80 is an FDA-approved emulsifier widely used in food at safe levels; its incidental use in some chemotherapy formulations does not make food containing it dangerous. The video and replies show the framing is moving people toward health-panic conclusions. A correction is genuinely useful.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note establishes BOTH: (a) DQ soft serve has always contained ~5% milkfat and never qualified as FDA 'ice cream' (which requires ≥10% milkfat) — this is not a recent change; AND (b) polysorbate 80 is an FDA-approved food emulsifier used at safe levels; its use in some drug formulations doesn't make food dangerous. Sources from FDA/eCFR/Snopes/Lead Stories acceptable. REJECT if the note endorses the 'chemo chemical' framing, agrees this is a recent FDA change, or fails to address either prong.
reference_note: Dairy Queen soft serve has always contained about 5% milkfat and never qualified as FDA 'ice cream' (which requires at least 10% milkfat) — this is not a recent change. Polysorbate 80 is an FDA-approved emulsifier used in frozen desserts at safe levels; its incidental use in some chemotherapy formulations does not make food containing it dangerous. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-135/subpart-B/section-135.110 https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-172/subpart-I/section-172.840 https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2022/07/fact-check-food-additives-found-in-dairy-queen-soft-serve-are-not-enough-to-cause-cancer-heart-disease.html

Notes that just say 'McCullough is wrong' without engaging the study he cites should NOT pass. Notes that endorse the DNA-alteration claim should fail.
reference_note: The Swedish study cited here does not show that mRNA COVID-19 vaccines alter human DNA. judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note OR writes a tightly factual note that accurately describes the state of the investigation. judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note; any note here is a false positive. why_note_decision: The quote is fabricated (no record Kid Rock said it), but the image is a self-evident satirical meme whose entire joke is geographic ignorance — Alaska IS in the United States, so 'leave the country and move to Alaska' is the punchline. The tweet's purpose is mockery, not to assert a genuine news quote, and top replies already treat it as obviously not real. A literal 'this quote is fabricated' note misreads transparent satire as a factual assertion.

Top replies recognize it isn't real. A note solemnly stating 'this quote is fabricated; Kid Rock made no such comment' treats obvious satire as a factual claim and is a false positive — FAIL it. Any note here fails.

tweet_summary: Border Patrol Union (NBPC) tweet defending Border Patrol agents in the Jan 24 2026 Minneapolis shooting of Alex Pretti, asserting he was a 'supposed peaceful protester' who brought a loaded handgun and 'brandished it,' justifying the shooting.
why_note_decision: The brandishing claim is materially disputed. NPR, eyewitnesses, and the Minneapolis Wikipedia article report that videos do NOT clearly show Pretti holding or brandishing a firearm — they show him recording with a phone, being pepper-sprayed, and being wrestled to the ground by ~6 agents before being shot ~10 times; one agent removed a handgun from his waistband before shots were fired. Trump and DHS officials say he was armed; the videos and eyewitness accounts contradict the 'brandished' framing. So the tweet's factual core ('brandished') is contested by direct video evidence, and a correct note is warranted. The original note FAILS this: it parrots the DHS account ('DHS confirmed… which he brandished') without surfacing the contradicting video evidence, and adds the body count of shots — making it neither a useful correction nor a useful confirmation. Many raters tagged it Incorrect (111), SourcesMissingOrUnreliable (91), MissingKeyPoints (97) — the note doesn't pass the test from EITHER direction.
judge_guidance: PASS the bot's note ONLY if it (a) flags that the 'brandished' framing is contested by available video and eyewitnesses (NPR coverage and the Wikipedia entry on the Jan 24 2026 Minneapolis ICE shooting are good anchors), (b) notes that an agent removed the holstered firearm from Pretti before shots were fired (per CNN/NPR/witness accounts), and (c) avoids endorsing either side as conclusively established. FAIL notes that simply restate DHS's claim that he 'brandished' a weapon (that's repeating the disputed assertion). FAIL notes that omit the video-contradiction entirely. FAIL notes that read as one-sided invective against Border Patrol. A correct note is bridging and source-anchored, not a re-litigation.
reference_note: Multiple videos and eyewitnesses (per NPR, CNN) contradict the Border Patrol Union's claim that Alex Pretti, the 37-year-old VA nurse killed Jan 24 2026, 'brandished' his firearm. Witnesses describe him recording on a phone; an agent is shown removing the handgun from his waistband before shots were fired. The DOJ and DHS investigation is ongoing. https://www.npr.org/2026/01/25/nx-s1-5687875/minneapolis-shooting-minnesota-ice-alex-pretti-dhs-investigation https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_24,_2026,_ICE_shooting_in_Minneapolis

AFP, PolitiFact, Newschecker and others all debunk this exact viral edit. The tweet pushes a clear conspiracy claim (ISS / spaceflight is fake) to ~3M views — a correction is warranted. The original note states the correct facts (cropped clip, ball pushed down, full video shows it returning) and cites NASA, AFP and a physics source; it just hasn't accumulated rater consensus, likely because conspiracy-aligned readers downvote correct corrections.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note (a) clearly states the viral clip is cropped/edited, (b) explains the astronaut pushed/threw the globe downward so it followed that trajectory (Newton's 1st law), and (c) ideally notes that in the full uncut NASA video the globe floats back up shortly after, and/or that microphones and other objects are seen floating. Strong notes cite AFP, PolitiFact, or the NASA ISS Expedition source video. FAIL if the bot writes a note that endorses or hedges the 'space is fake' framing, fails to mention the cropping/edit, or merely says 'physics is real' without addressing the specific clip. FAIL if the bot declines to write a note (the claim is a checkable, high-reach conspiracy).

judge_guidance: PASS only if the note gives the correct arithmetic: people born in 2016 turn 10 in 2026 (2026 - 2016 = 10), and ideally adds that turning 16 in 2026 implies a 2010 birth year. It must be concise and clearly state the right numbers. FAIL if the note repeats or endorses the false '16' figure, hedges without committing to the correct answer, or muddles the years.
reference_note: People born in 2016 are turning 10 in 2026, not 16. Someone turning 16 in 2026 would have been born in 2010.    https://www.calculator.net/age-calculator.html
importance_lens_rationale: 2.3M impressions but trivial arithmetic with no real-world stakes; useful only as a clean, unambiguous numeric-correction example for the bot.

The correct answer is no note — any note that picks a side fails.

why_note_decision: Multiple material inaccuracies in a high-reach (957k impressions, 6.3k likes) health/science claim: (1) the drug is LOY-002, not 'LOT-002' (LOT-006-002 is just the trial bottle label visible in the video); (2) Loyal targets ~1 year of additional healthy lifespan in senior dogs (10+ years old, 14+ lb), not 'many years'; (3) the drug is still in FDA review — only two of three required technical sections accepted as of the tweet date, the final review is expected in 2027 but the drug isn't approved or on the market. Worth correcting both for science accuracy and to manage expectations of grieving pet owners (visible in comments) who might be misled about timing or efficacy.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note corrects at least two of: (a) the drug name (LOY-002, not LOT-002), (b) the magnitude of lifespan extension (~1 year of healthy lifespan in senior dogs, NOT 'many years'), (c) the regulatory status (still in FDA conditional-approval review, not yet approved or available to consumers, 2027 is a target for final review not market launch). Sources should include Loyal's own posts or reputable veterinary press (dvm360, Veterinary Practice News). FAIL if the note (a) accepts 'many years lifespan extension' as accurate, (b) implies the drug is already approved or available, or (c) only nitpicks the typo without addressing the overstated efficacy claim.
reference_note: The drug is LOY-002 (the tweet's 'LOT-002' is the trial bottle code) by the company Loyal. It is still in FDA conditional-approval review — two of three required technical sections accepted, with the final section expected to be reviewed in 2027 (not on-market by 2027). Loyal targets ~1 additional year of healthy lifespan for senior dogs (10+ years old, 14+ lb), not 'many years'. https://loyal.com/posts/loy-002-tas https://www.dvm360.com/view/lifespan-extension-drug-in-development-for-senior-dogs-reaches-a-new-milestone
original_note_text: The drug is LOY-002 (not LOT-002) by Loyal, still in FDA clinical trials seeking conditional approval and not yet available; it targets ~1.8 years healthy lifespan extension in senior dogs (10+ years, 14+ lb), not many years. https://loyal.com/posts/loy-002-tas https://loyal.com/posts/metabolic-dysfunction
failure_reason: Note has the right facts but very low rating volume (only 16 ratings, dominant 'note not needed' at just 3). Probably hasn't reached enough raters yet rather than being content-failed. The note is substantively accurate; the '1.8 years' figure may be slightly high vs. published 'around a year' — worth verifying. Citing only loyal.com (the company's own site) twice reduces source diversity.
importance_lens_rationale: Health/science claim from a 1.7M-follower account about pet longevity, with emotionally vulnerable audience (visible in comments). Correcting overhyped lifespan claims is moderately valuable; not high-stakes but matters for science communication and pet-owner expectations.

tweet_summary: Rep. Nancy Mace claims President Trump 'ended eight wars in eight months,' calling him the 'President of Peace.'
why_note_decision: The 'eight wars in eight months' figure is a specific, checkable claim that major fact-checkers (CNN, AP/US News, Axios) have found to be a significant exaggeration: the list counts non-wars (e.g. the Egypt-Ethiopia dam dispute) and conflicts that did not actually end (DRC-Rwanda, Thailand-Cambodia flared again), and parties disputed US involvement (India-Pakistan). A clarifying note benefits the 193k+ readers, so a note IS warranted — contrary to the provisional no-note label.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (1) addresses the specific 'eight wars in eight months' figure and explains it is an overstatement, citing concrete examples (e.g. the Egypt-Ethiopia matter is a diplomatic dam dispute not a war; the DRC-Rwanda and Thailand-Cambodia conflicts continued after the announced deals; India disputed US mediation), and (2) attributes this to named fact-checks (AP, CNN, Axios). It must AVOID the original note's failures: do not be vaguely argumentative ('multiple fact-checkers found no evidence...') without specifics, and do not cite a single possibly-wrong URL. It should be neutral and factual, not a partisan rebuttal of whether Trump deserves credit at all. A note that just says 'this is false/opinion' without enumerating the actual problems is too weak.
reference_note: The 'eight wars in eight months' figure is disputed by fact-checkers. The list counts a non-war (the Egypt-Ethiopia Nile dam diplomatic dispute) and conflicts that did not actually end: fighting in the DRC-Rwanda and Thailand-Cambodia conflicts resumed after the announced agreements, and India rejected US mediation of its Pakistan ceasefire. Trump played a diplomatic role in several, but 'ended eight wars' overstates both the count and the permanence. https://apnews.com/article/fact-check-trump-eight-wars-ended https://www.axios.com/2025/10/10/gaza-trump-wars-ended-israel-nobel-prize
original_note_text: Misleading: multiple fact-checkers found no evidence Trump 'ended eight wars in eight months.' Several cited conflicts continued or were limited diplomatic shifts/ceasefires, not full war endings. See CNN fact-check: https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/03/politics/fact-check-trump-cbs-interview
failure_reason: Vague and lightly sourced: 'multiple fact-checkers found no evidence' with no specific examples, and the single CNN URL (dated 11/03) is unverifiable / does not resolve to the relevant fact-check (the actual CNN/AP checks are dated Oct & Dec 2025). Reporters tagged it OpinionSpeculation/ArgumentativeOrBiased because it reads as assertion rather than enumerated evidence.
importance_lens_rationale: A sitting US Representative amplifying a quantified foreign-policy claim to 540k followers; accurate accounting of war/peace outcomes is high-value for the public's grasp of geopolitics.

why_note_decision: The image fabricates a JFK quote/endorsement that he never made. AIPAC is a US-registered domestic lobby, not a foreign agent. judge_guidance: PASS criteria: (1) Note must say the JFK 'AIPAC IS A FOREIGN AGENT' quote/sign is fabricated — JFK never publicly said or signed this. (2) Should note the related actual history: under JFK, the DOJ (led by RFK) asked AIPAC's predecessor the American Zionist Council to register as a foreign agent in 1962; the effort was dropped by 1965. reference_note: The image is fabricated; JFK never made this statement or signed any such sign. The Kennedy administration's DOJ (under AG Robert Kennedy) asked AIPAC's predecessor, the American Zionist Council, to register as a foreign agent in 1962, but that requirement was abandoned by 1965. AIPAC is registered as a domestic US lobby. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Zionist_Council https://www.wrmea.org/jfk-assassination/robert-kennedy-s-attempt-to-register-aipac-as-a-foreign-agent.html
original_note_text: JFK never made this statement. failure_reason: Substance correct but missing key point — the image itself is fabricated/AI-woodcut, not just the words. The note also fails to make AIPAC's current status (US-registered domestic lobby) clear, which is the real-world misimpression the tweet creates.
importance_lens_rationale: Fabricated historical-quote images on geopolitical lobby topics drive durable false beliefs; correcting matters for political discourse quality.

tweet_summary: Texas state Rep. James Talarico (running for US Senate) says 'Trump's FCC refused to air my interview with Stephen Colbert' on The Late Show; posts a video clip from the show.
why_note_decision: Tweet is editorializing around a real event. What actually happened: CBS network lawyers told The Late Show the interview could not air on broadcast because doing so would trigger the FCC equal-time rule for Talarico's primary opponents (per FCC Chair Brendan Carr's January guidance). Colbert himself blamed the FCC and Trump on-air; CBS denied the FCC 'prohibited' it but acknowledged the legal advice was in response to FCC guidance. The dispute is over the framing word 'refused' (Talarico says FCC, CBS says CBS lawyers acting on FCC guidance). This is a textbook insider_reporting_framing case — the underlying facts (interview not aired on broadcast, posted to YouTube, FCC equal-time guidance triggered the decision) are reported in NYT, WaPo, CNN, PBS, NBC, CBS itself, Forbes. The original AI note tries to thread the needle ('CBS did not air... due to legal concerns from recent FCC guidance... FCC did not directly block it') which is technically accurate but reads as a partisan correction of a half-true framing; raters slammed it notHelpfulMissingKeyPoints 834, notHelpfulNoteNotNeeded 701. Better to decline.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The dispute here is purely about whether 'FCC refused to air' is fair shorthand for 'CBS lawyers pulled it citing FCC equal-time guidance from Trump-appointed Chair Carr' — that is framing, not fact. The underlying events (interview pulled from broadcast, posted to YouTube, FCC equal-time rule cited as reason) are well-reported and not in dispute. Any note that tries to 'correct' Talarico by saying CBS, not FCC, made the call is missing the point that CBS made the call BECAUSE of FCC guidance. If the bot writes a note, it's a false positive.
original_note_text: CBS did not air the interview on The Late Show due to legal concerns from recent FCC guidance on equal time rules by Chair Brendan Carr. The FCC did not directly block it. Full interview is on The Late Show's YouTube channel.    https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2026/02/17/colbert-says-cbs-refused-to-air-his-interview-with-democrat-candidate-fearing-fcc-blowback    https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/17/arts/television/colbert-fcc-trump-talarico-cbs.html    https://deadline.com/2026/02/stephen-colbert-cbs-james-talarico-interview-1236726609/
failure_reason: Pedantic framing correction. Tries to draw a line between 'CBS lawyers' and 'FCC' when the actual chain is 'CBS lawyers acted because of FCC equal-time guidance from a Trump-appointed chair' — which is what Talarico is summarizing. Raters tagged notHelpfulMissingKeyPoints (834) and notHelpfulNoteNotNeeded (701).
importance_lens_rationale: Press-freedom / media-regulation story (14M views, US Senate candidate) — the cost of pedantic notes 'correcting' a defensible framing is high; they make the notewriter look like a White House defender.

tweet_summary: A journalist posts a two-photo composite (a soldier holding a pistol to a young Black man's head; a soldier kicking a Black child) captioned 'This is how the US wants to bring freedom to Venezuela,' implying US forces abusing Venezuelans.
why_note_decision: The images are real but grossly miscontextualized: they are from the 1993 UN peacekeeping mission in Somalia, NOT Venezuela and NOT US soldiers. As replies and historical records confirm, these depict the 'Somalia Affair' abuses by CANADIAN (Airborne Regiment, torture/killing of teenager Shidane Arone) and BELGIAN paratroopers. So a note is clearly warranted. The original note's MissingKeyPoints/Incorrect failure: it mislabels the events as the 'Battle of Mogadishu' and frames the soldiers as engaged in '1993 operations against Somali militia' — implying US Black Hawk Down forces — when the perpetrators were Canadian and Belgian peacekeepers committing documented abuses against civilians. The country/era (Somalia, 1993) is right; the actors and the specific incident are wrong.
judge_guidance: A correct note must establish that (1) the photos are NOT from Venezuela and do NOT show US soldiers, and (2) they depict 1993 UN peacekeeping abuses in Somalia — the top image associated with the Canadian 'Somalia Affair' (Canadian Airborne Regiment) and the bottom with Belgian paratroopers. PASS only if it correctly attributes the soldiers as Canadian/Belgian peacekeepers in Somalia and disclaims the Venezuela/US framing. FAIL if it repeats the original note's error of calling it the 'Battle of Mogadishu' or implying these were US forces / US operations against militia — that misattribution is the specific failure to avoid. Saying merely 'old Somalia footage' without correcting the US-soldier implication is insufficient given the tweet's core claim is about US forces.
reference_note: These photos are not from Venezuela and do not show US soldiers. They are from the 1993 UN peacekeeping mission in Somalia: the abuses were committed by Canadian (the 'Somalia Affair', Canadian Airborne Regiment) and Belgian paratroopers against Somali civilians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia_affair https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/somalia-affair
original_note_text: Images show 1990s Battle of Mogadishu in Somalia, not Venezuela. Soldiers wear desert camouflage from 1993 operations against Somali militia, documented in historical records of that conflict. https://www.armytimes.com/news/your-army/2023/11/06/forgotten-bastards-battle-of-mogadishus-unsung-heroes-await-honors/
failure_reason: Incorrect/MissingKeyPoints: wrongly labels the scenes as the 'Battle of Mogadishu' and '1993 operations against Somali militia' (which evokes US Black Hawk Down forces). The actual perpetrators were Canadian and Belgian UN peacekeepers abusing civilians (the Somalia Affair), and it cites an irrelevant US-Army article.
importance_lens_rationale: 1.8M impressions; correcting fabricated atrocity attribution during a tense Venezuela-US period reduces inflammatory geopolitical misinformation.

tweet_summary: Football transfer-rumor account indykaila claims Xabi Alonso's reps told Liverpool that Chelsea are making enquiries, and that his first choice is Liverpool.
why_note_decision: This is a transfer rumor from an aggregator account. Fabrizio Romano in May 2026 confirms Chelsea met directly with Alonso and Liverpool has not approached his camp — but Romano cannot rule out that Alonso's reps did a back-channel signal to Liverpool, which is exactly the kind of unverifiable insider sourcing transfer reporters trade in. The original note overreaches by treating Romano's 'no Liverpool approach' line as a debunk of a different claim (reps informing Liverpool of Chelsea's interest). It is a framing dispute over a low-stakes rumor, not a factual misrepresentation a reader needs corrected.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. This is a routine transfer-rumor tweet from an aggregator account. Any note here is a false positive — the claim is unverifiable insider sourcing, the consequences are trivial sports gossip, and the original (NOT_HELPFUL) note over-applied Romano's quote to debunk a slightly different claim. FAIL any note that asserts Liverpool has not been contacted by Alonso's reps (that's an unverifiable negative).
